---
title: "Quiz: segmentation networks"
---

Short questions on encoder–decoders, U-Nets, per-pixel losses and evaluation. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Dice $= 2|P \cap G|/(|P| + |G|)$, IoU $= |P \cap G|/|P \cup G|$.

---

**Q1.** Why can a classification network with a dense last layer not simply be used to segment an image?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does it output, and for which input size?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It outputs one set of class probabilities for the whole image, and its dense layer fixes the input size. A segmentation network must output one probability per pixel, for any image size: it has to be convolutional all the way, with a decoder that returns to full resolution.
:::

---

**Q2.** What do the skip connections of a U-Net carry, and what goes wrong without them?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What did pooling throw away?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
They copy the sharp, full-resolution feature maps of the encoder to the decoder. Without them the decoder only has the coarse bottleneck maps: it knows roughly where objects are, but boundaries and small objects come out blurred or misplaced.
:::

---

**Q3.** Nuclei cover 3 % of the pixels. A network predicts "background" everywhere. What are its pixel accuracy and its Dice?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$|P| = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Accuracy 97 %, Dice 0 (no true positives). Accuracy rewards the large background class; Dice looks only at the objects.
:::

---

**Q4.** Upsample $(4, 8)$ by a factor 2 with nearest neighbour, then with a transposed convolution with stride 2 and kernel $(\tfrac12, 1, \tfrac12)$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each input value stamps the scaled kernel, two positions apart.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Nearest: $(4, 4, 8, 8)$. Transposed: $4 \cdot (\tfrac12, 1, \tfrac12)$ at positions 0–2 and $8 \cdot (\tfrac12, 1, \tfrac12)$ at positions 2–4: $(2, 4, 2 + 4, 8, 4) = (2, 4, 6, 8, 4)$: linear interpolation between 4 and 8, with a half value at the far end.
:::

---

**Q5.** A U-Net trained on images from one microscope gives Dice 0.95 on held-out images from it, and 0.6 on images from a new microscope. What is this called, and what would you do?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Training range.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Domain shift: the new images (brightness, noise, blur, stain) lie outside what the network has seen. Annotate a few images from the new microscope and add them to the training set (fine-tune), augment brightness and noise more strongly during training, and always test on images from the setting where the network will be used.
:::

---

**Q6.** The U-Net gives a perfect mask of two touching nuclei. Why is the nucleus count still wrong?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Connected components of the mask.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A semantic mask only says "nucleus or not" per pixel: two touching nuclei form one connected component, which labelling counts as one object. They have to be split, for example with a "boundary" class, the distance transform and the watershed (days 8–10), or with a network that outputs separate objects (day 18).
:::

---

**Q7.** *(math)* Soft Dice $D = 2\sum p_ig_i/(\sum p_i + \sum g_i)$. A pixel outside the object ($g_j = 0$) has its probability $p_j$ raised. Does $D$ go up or down? Show it from the formula.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Only the denominator depends on $p_j$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Down: with $g_j = 0$ the numerator does not change and the denominator grows, $\partial D/\partial p_j = -2\sum_i p_ig_i/(\sum_i p_i + \sum_i g_i)^2 \le 0$. False positives are penalised, and more strongly the better the overlap already is.
:::
